topics: Front matter, printed pp. ix–xi — List of Exercises: Chapter 1 has eleven analytical and three computer exercises; Chapter 2 has eighteen analytical and five computer exercises.

Preface, printed pp. xiii–xv — Scope, intended senior-undergraduate/first-year-graduate audience, concise main path versus advanced complements, MATLAB experiments, prerequisites, and the nonparametric/parametric organization.

§1.1 Introduction, pp. 1–3 — Spectral estimation as recovery of power distribution over frequency from a finite stationary record; applications; nonparametric versus parametric approaches; complex discrete signals.
§1.2 Energy Spectral Density of Deterministic Signals, pp. 3–4 — DTFT/inverse DTFT, Parseval, energy density, projection interpretation, and autocorrelation transform.

§1.3 Power Spectral Density of Random Signals, pp. 4–8 — second-order stationarity, autocovariance sequence and Toeplitz covariance matrix, two equivalent PSD definitions, and frequency units/aliasing.
§1.3.1 First Definition of PSD, pp. 6–7 — PSD as the DTFT of the autocovariance sequence and total average power as its integral.
§1.3.2 Second Definition of PSD, pp. 7–8 — PSD as the limiting expected normalized squared finite-record Fourier magnitude.
§1.4 Properties of PSDs, pp. 8–11 — nonnegativity, periodicity, real-signal even symmetry, covariance-convention subtlety, LTI filtering law, and modulation-induced frequency shift.
§1.5 The Spectral Estimation Problem, p. 12 — estimating a continuous PSD from N samples and the practical limitation imposed by short stationary observation intervals.
§1.6.1 Coherency Spectrum, pp. 12–14 — normalized cross-spectrum, least-squares residual interpretation, unit bound, perfect linear dependence, and invariance under stable filtering.

§1.7 Exercises, pp. 14–21 — frequency-axis scaling, time-frequency marginals, ACS validity/positivity, correlated filtering, least-squares spectral approximation, Wiener–Hopf filtering, two-sided FFT handling, and covariance-eigenvalue experiments.
§2.1 Introduction, p. 22 — classical nonparametric estimators and the fundamental variance-versus-resolution motivation for refined methods.
§2.2 Periodogram and Correlogram Methods, pp. 22–25 — periodogram, biased and unbiased covariance estimates, periodogram–correlogram equivalence, and intuition for failure.
§2.3 Periodogram Computation via FFT, pp. 25–28 — DFT sampling, radix-2 decimation, operation count, zero padding, and FFT pruning.

§2.4.1 Bias Analysis of the Periodogram, pp. 28–32 — expectation as convolution with the Fejér/Bartlett spectral window, Dirichlet alternative, smearing, leakage, resolution, and asymptotic unbiasedness.
§2.4.2 Variance Analysis of the Periodogram, pp. 32–37 — circular Gaussian white noise, fourth-order moment factorization, asymptotic covariance, filtered-noise extension, and inconsistency.
§2.5 Blackman–Tukey Method, pp. 37–40 — lag-windowed covariance estimate, local frequency averaging, resolution/variance scaling, and conditions guaranteeing a nonnegative spectrum.
§2.6.1 Time–Bandwidth Product and Resolution–Variance Tradeoffs, pp. 40–41 — equivalent duration and bandwidth, unit product, window-length choice, and smearing/leakage tradeoff.
§2.6.2 Some Common Lag Windows, pp. 41–45 — rectangular, Bartlett, Hann, Hamming, Blackman, Chebyshev, and Kaiser windows with main-lobe and sidelobe comparisons.
§2.6.3 Window Design Example, pp. 45–47 — positive-semidefinite spectral-window construction and dominant-eigenvector design that minimizes relative sidelobe energy.
§2.6.4 Temporal Windows and Lag Windows, pp. 47–48 — matched temporal/lag autocorrelation windows and equality of their mean spectral behavior.
§2.7.1 Bartlett Method, pp. 49–50 — averaging nonoverlapping segment periodograms, equivalent covariance view, and the factor-L resolution/variance exchange.
§2.7.2 Welch Method, pp. 50–52 — overlapped tapered segments, normalization, averaging, decorrelation intuition, and approximate Blackman–Tukey form.
§2.7.3 Daniell Method, pp. 52–55 — local frequency averaging, frequency-sample correlation, rectangular spectral window, and sinc lag window.
§2.8.1–2.8.2 Complements, pp. 55–59 — FFT computation of sample covariances and windowed Blackman–Tukey estimates.
§2.8.3 Apodization, pp. 59–64 — data- and frequency-dependent temporal windows from constrained least squares, leakage reduction without resolution loss, and an adjacent-bin FFT implementation.
§2.8.4 Cross-Spectra and Coherency, pp. 64–66 — failure of raw periodogram coherency, lag-window centering for cross-covariance, and smoothed cross-periodograms.
§2.8.5 More Time–Bandwidth Product Results, pp. 66–71 — generalized duration-bandwidth inequalities, uncertainty interpretation, and variance-based widths.
§2.9 Analytical Exercises, pp. 71–79 — unknown means, negative unbiased correlograms, finite-sample covariance, shrinkage, dB uncertainty, exact variance, and window optimality.

§2.9 Computer Exercises, pp. 79–85 — zero-padding demonstrations, two-tone resolution/leakage, Monte Carlo bias/variance, refined estimator comparison, and spectral analysis of measured sunspot and lynx data.
key_results: Spectral estimation is formally the problem of using a finite record y(1),…,y(N) from a second-order stationary process to estimate its PSD φ(ω) over −π≤ω≤π. The common practical bottleneck is not computation but the short interval over which stationarity is credible. [§1.5, p. 12]

For a deterministic finite-energy sequence, S(ω)=|Y(ω)|² is the energy spectral density and Parseval gives Σt|y(t)|²=(1/2π)∫S(ω)dω. The same S is the DTFT of the deterministic autocorrelation ρ(k)=Σt y(t)y*(t−k). [§1.2, pp. 3–4]

A zero-mean process is second-order stationary when r(k)=E{y(t)y*(t−k)} depends only on lag. Its autocovariance is conjugate symmetric, r(k)=r*(−k), and |r(k)|≤r(0). Every finite Toeplitz covariance matrix formed from r is positive semidefinite. [§1.3, pp. 5–6]

The first PSD definition is the Wiener–Khinchin transform pair φ(ω)=Σk r(k)e^(−iωk) and r(k)=(1/2π)∫φ(ω)e^(iωk)dω. Consequently r(0), the average signal power, equals the integral of the PSD. [§1.3.1, pp. 6–7]
The second PSD definition is φ(ω)=lim(N→∞)E{|Σ(t=1 to N)y(t)e^(−iωt)|²/N}. It equals the covariance-transform definition when (1/N)Σ(k=−N to N)|k||r(k)|→0. [§1.3.2, pp. 7–8]
A discrete-time PSD is real, nonnegative, and 2π-periodic. It is even for real-valued processes but need not be even for complex processes. [§§1.3–1.4, pp. 8–9]

The authors stress a convention-dependent subtlety: φ(ω) is strictly the spectral content of the chosen autocovariance sequence. Defining covariance with the opposite lag reverses the spectrum, which matters for complex signals. [§1.4, pp. 9–10]
For stationary e(t) passed through an asymptotically stable LTI system H, the output PSD is φy(ω)=|H(ω)|²φe(ω). Complex modulation y(t)=e^(iω0t)x(t) shifts the PSD: φy(ω)=φx(ω−ω0). [§1.4, pp. 10–11]

Nonparametric methods assume no functional form for φ; parametric methods estimate a finite model. Parametric methods can be more accurate when the model is right but are sensitive to misspecification, so nonparametric methods remain competitive even under plausible models. [§1.1, pp. 1–2; §1.5, p. 12]

Complex coherency is Cyu(ω)=φyu(ω)/sqrt(φyy(ω)φuu(ω)). Its magnitude is at most one and weights the least-squares residual power through E|ε|²=(1/2π)∫[1−|Cyu|²]φyy dω. Unit magnitude everywhere means exact mean-square linear dependence. [§1.6.1, pp. 12–13]

The magnitude of coherency is unchanged if y and u are passed through arbitrary stable filters, even different ones. It is therefore the frequency-domain analogue of a scale-invariant correlation coefficient. [§1.6.1, pp. 13–14]
Changing from normalized angular frequency ω to physical angular frequency ω̄=ω/Ts requires a density Jacobian: φ̄(ω̄)=Tsφ(ω̄Ts), not mere argument substitution. [Exercise 1.1, pp. 14–15]

A sequence is a valid ACS exactly when every finite Toeplitz matrix formed from it is positive semidefinite, equivalently when its Fourier transform is nonnegative for every frequency. Simple truncation of a valid ACS can violate this property. [Exercises 1.7–1.8, p. 16]
The Wiener–Hopf relation φyu(ω)=H(ω)φuu(ω) holds both when y is literally the output of H driven by u and when H is the unrestricted LTI filter minimizing E|y−H*u|². [Exercise 1.11, p. 18]
The periodogram drops the unattainable expectation and limit from the second PSD definition: φ̂p(ω)=|Σ(t=1 to N)y(t)e^(−iωt)|²/N. [§2.2.1, p. 22]

The standard unbiased covariance divides a lag-k product sum by N−k; the standard biased estimate divides by N. Despite its name, the biased estimate is usually preferred because high-lag values are damped and the complete sequence is guaranteed positive semidefinite. [§2.2.2, pp. 23–24]

The correlogram computed from the standard biased ACS is exactly the periodogram. This identity connects a squared finite-record transform to the transform of its sample autocovariance and lets both estimators share one analysis. [§2.2.2, p. 24]
An N-point radix-2 FFT uses about (1/2)Nlog2N complex flops versus order N² for direct DFT evaluation; the split-radix comparison quoted is about (1/3)Nlog2N. [§2.3.1, pp. 26–27]

Zero padding samples the same continuous-frequency periodogram more densely. It can reveal the shape between original Fourier bins but cannot improve the estimator’s true spectral resolution. [§2.3.2, pp. 27–28]
MSE decomposes into variance plus squared bias. This decomposition makes clear that a lower-variance refined periodogram may have greater total error if its smoothing bias is too large. [§2.4, p. 28]
The expected periodogram is the true PSD convolved with the Fejér kernel WB(ω)=(1/N)[sin(Nω/2)/sin(ω/2)]², the DTFT of the Bartlett lag window. [§2.4.1, pp. 28–30]

The Fejér main lobe smears neighboring peaks; its sidelobes leak strong-band power into weak or empty bands. The periodogram’s resolution limit is about 1/N cycles per sampling interval, and leakage is especially destructive for large-dynamic-range spectra. [§2.4.1, pp. 30–32]
The periodogram is unbiased for white noise and asymptotically unbiased for a broad class of spectra, but this does not make it a good estimator. [§2.4.1, p. 32]

For circular Gaussian white noise, asymptotic periodogram values at distinct frequencies are uncorrelated, while var{φ̂p(ω)}→φ²(ω). The same result extends to general stable linear processes driven by such noise. [§2.4.2, pp. 32–36]
Because its asymptotic standard deviation equals the PSD itself rather than shrinking with N, the raw periodogram is inconsistent and remains erratic for arbitrarily long records. [§2.4.2, p. 36]

The Blackman–Tukey estimate φ̂BT(ω)=Σ(|k|<M)w(k)r̂(k)e^(−iωk) discards inaccurate high lags and is equivalently a local spectral-window average of the periodogram. Its resolution scales as 1/M and variance as M/N. [§2.5.1, pp. 37–38]

If the lag window is positive semidefinite, so W(ω)≥0, then its Hadamard product with the biased sample covariance remains positive semidefinite and the Blackman–Tukey spectrum is nonnegative. Rectangular lag windows lack this guarantee; Bartlett has it. [§2.5.2, p. 39]

For regular nonnegative window pairs, equivalent duration Ne and bandwidth βe satisfy Neβe=1. Thus window length controls resolution, while M/N controls variance; the stated rule of thumb M≤N/10 reduces standard deviation by at least about three relative to the periodogram. [§2.6.1, pp. 40–41]

At fixed length and w(0), main-lobe and sidelobe energy cannot both be reduced. Window length negotiates resolution versus variance, while window shape negotiates smearing versus leakage. [§2.6.1, p. 41]

For common lag windows, approximate main-lobe width/sidelobe level progresses from rectangular 2π/M and −13 dB through Bartlett/Hann/Hamming near 4π/M and −25/−31/−41 dB to Blackman 6π/M and −57 dB. [§2.6.2, pp. 41–44]

Kaiser γ continuously trades main-lobe width for sidelobe level; Chebyshev makes sidelobes equiripple. Except for Bartlett, the listed fixed windows are not guaranteed to have nonnegative Fourier transforms, but convolving a window with itself creates a positive-semidefinite lag window. [§2.6.2, pp. 41–44]

The leakage-minimizing positive spectral window W=|V|² is obtained by choosing v as the dominant eigenvector of Γ, whose entries are βsinc[(m−n)βπ], then setting w to the autocorrelation of v. This maximizes energy inside |ω|≤βπ. [§2.6.3, pp. 45–47]

A temporal taper v and lag window w=(1/N)(v*v-reversed) produce windowed periodogram and Blackman–Tukey estimators with the same expected spectrum, though not the same realization. [§2.6.4, pp. 47–48]

Bartlett averages L=N/M nonoverlapping M-sample periodograms. Relative to the raw periodogram it reduces both variance and resolution by roughly L, and it is slightly less statistically efficient than a rectangular-window Blackman–Tukey estimate because it discards available lag products. [§2.7.1, pp. 49–50]

Welch improves Bartlett by overlapping segments (commonly 50%) and tapering each before averaging. Overlap supplies more averages; tapering controls bias and downweights shared endpoints, though its variance advantage over Bartlett is usually modest. [§2.7.2, pp. 50–52]

Daniell locally averages periodogram values and is a Blackman–Tukey estimator with a rectangular spectral window and sinc lag window. More zero-padded bins do not create more independent averages: adjacent bins become correlated. [§2.7.3, pp. 52–54]

Periodogram, Blackman–Tukey, Bartlett, Welch, and Daniell are variations on one theme: smooth or average an inconsistent periodogram to reduce variance, necessarily paying with bias or resolution. [§2.8 opening, p. 55]

All N biased sample covariance lags can be computed using a zero-padded FFT, squared magnitudes, and inverse FFT. The rough full-lag crossover favors this over direct order-N²/2 calculation for N at least about 32, subject to implementation details. [§2.8.1, pp. 55–56]

A general windowed Blackman–Tukey estimate needs three FFTs in the presented implementation: two for the sample covariance and one for its windowed transform. An exact discrete spectral-window sum is preferable for special windows such as Daniell’s. [§2.8.2, pp. 57–59]

Apodization chooses a nonnegative, unity-sum temporal window separately for each frequency and dataset by minimizing the fitted sinusoid’s residual output power. Interpreted as a filter, it passes the target sinusoid undistorted and suppresses the other observed components. [§2.8.3, pp. 59–62]

With the one-parameter cosine window, apodization reduces to combining DFT bin k with its two neighbors using a clipped β∈[0,1]. It therefore cuts leakage while retaining periodogram resolution for only marginal extra computation. [§2.8.3, pp. 62–64]
Raw bivariate periodogram coherency is identically one because the 2×2 matrix ZZ*/N has rank one. A meaningful coherency estimate requires spectral smoothing/windowing. [§2.8.4, p. 64]

Cross-covariance need not be even or peak at zero. A short lag window must be centered near its essential lag k0; a poor center either excludes informative lags (bias) or admits noisy high-order lags (variance). [§2.8.4, pp. 64–66]

For broad classes of sequences, generalized duration and bandwidth obey N̄eβ̄e≥1. With energy-variance definitions and mild centering/boundary conditions, Ñeβ̃e≥1/(4π), strengthened by a phase-slope covariance term. [§2.8.5, pp. 66–71]

The book warns that nonparametric time–bandwidth resolution is a limitation of an analysis approach, not necessarily of the signal itself; later parametric methods can resolve structure on scales smaller than 1/Ne when their model is justified. [§2.8.5, p. 68]

For a Gaussian process the exact finite-sample periodogram covariance is |a*(μ)Ra(ν)|²/N². A practical separation exceeding about 4π/N makes two periodogram values nearly uncorrelated; asymptotic independence claims alone conceal this finite-sample scale. [Exercise 2.13, pp. 75–76]

For asymptotically unbiased periodogram estimates with variance φ², multiplying by 1/2 minimizes MSE and halves it—an intentionally stark example in which adding bias improves estimation. [Exercise 2.10, pp. 74–75]
If refined spectral-estimate variance is proportional to φ²(ω), expressing power in dB makes the asymptotic confidence-band width independent of the unknown PSD level. [Exercise 2.12, p. 75]
pedagogy: The book is deliberately concise but rigorous, intended for senior undergraduates, first-year graduate students, and self-study. The main narrative introduces definitions, derives estimator identities, and immediately interprets each equation statistically or physically; advanced complements can be skipped on a first pass. Chapters 1–2 assume discrete-time LTI systems, elementary stochastic processes, Fourier methods, and basic linear algebra, while estimation theory is helpful but not required. The teaching sequence is unusually coherent: define PSD in two ways, derive the two basic estimators from those definitions, prove they coincide, diagnose their bias and variance, then show how every classical refinement moves along the same bias–variance–resolution surface. Thirty-seven exercises in this shard mix proofs, counterexamples, derivations, and MATLAB investigations. Analytical problems are roughly ordered by difficulty and sometimes develop results absent from the main text; computer exercises use Monte Carlo trials and parameter sweeps to make leakage, resolution, and inconsistency visible. The measured-data exercise deliberately leaves preprocessing and estimator choice open. Figures are mostly paired time/frequency window plots and estimator comparisons, designed to be regenerated rather than reproduced.

gems: The preface traces ‘spectrum’ from Newton’s prism to the Latin ‘specter,’ then jokes that the student should be a vivid presence rather than a ghostly apparition. [Preface, p. xiii]

One sentence defines the entire field: from a finite stationary record, estimate how total power is distributed over frequency. The wording keeps finiteness and stationarity—often hidden assumptions—front and center. [§1.1, p. 1]

The application roll call spans machine wear, economic cycles, meteorology, astronomy, speech, radar/sonar, ECG/EEG diagnosis, earthquakes and volcanoes, oil exploration, and control-system identification. [§1.1, p. 1]

Complex signals can be simpler than real ones: a real sinusoid is two constrained complex exponentials, while one complex sinusoid is unconstrained and often directly available as I/Q data. [§1.1, pp. 2–3]

The PSD convention caveat is a useful conceptual trap: reversing the autocovariance lag reverses a complex process’s spectrum, so ‘power in the signal at ω’ is not entirely convention-free. [§1.4, pp. 9–10]
Why records stay short even when storage is cheap: the process itself may only be stationary for a short interval. More samples can violate the premise rather than improve the estimate. [§1.5, p. 12]

Coherency is made tangible by regression error: |C(ω)| tells how much of y at each frequency can be explained by a linear filter of u, and remains unchanged under stable filtering of either signal. [§1.6.1, pp. 12–14]

The least-squares FIR spectral approximation exercise reveals a seductive failure: truncating the true covariance minimizes integrated squared spectral error in covariance coordinates, but the truncated sequence may cease to be a valid covariance and produce negative ‘power.’ [Exercise 1.10, pp. 17–18]
The two-sided FFT exercise deliberately invites the wrong ordering, then shows that taking real(fft(z)) can hide a circular-shift error rather than fix roundoff. [Exercise C1.13, pp. 19–20]
A 256×256 covariance matrix’s eigenvalue distribution approaches the distribution of sampled PSD values—an empirical bridge between Toeplitz linear algebra and spectrum. [Exercise C1.14, pp. 20–21]
The periodogram’s historical name comes from Schuster’s 1900 search for hidden periodicities, exactly the task it still visually suggests. [§2.2.1, p. 22]

The ‘biased’ covariance estimate is usually the better scientific object: it behaves at large lags and guarantees a nonnegative periodogram, while the ‘unbiased’ estimate can explode from a single product and yield negative power. [§2.2.2, pp. 23–24]

The periodogram’s failure is summarized as estimating a variance from one filtered sample. Longer records supply more frequencies, not repeated evidence at each frequency, so the fluctuations do not vanish. [§§2.2–2.4, pp. 25, 36]

Zero padding is an interpolation lens, not a resolution microscope: it reveals the already-existing curve between DFT bins but cannot split features the finite observation merged. [§2.3.2, p. 27; Exercise C2.19, p. 80]
Smearing and leakage are separated cleanly: main lobes merge nearby components; sidelobes let strong distant components impersonate weak local power. [§2.4.1, pp. 30–32]

The raw periodogram is asymptotically unbiased yet inconsistent—a memorable warning that bias alone is a terrible quality metric. Its standard deviation approaches the true PSD value itself. [§2.4, pp. 32–36]
The rule M≤N/10 turns an abstract tradeoff into a concrete first move: accept roughly tenfold poorer lag aperture to cut spectral-estimate standard deviation by at least about three. [§2.6.1, p. 41]
The window table makes every designer pay visibly: rectangular gets a 2π/M main lobe but only −13 dB sidelobes; Blackman reaches −57 dB by widening to 6π/M. [§2.6.2, p. 42]

The weak-signal/strong-interferer design example chooses leakage over resolution because the two signals are already well separated. It is a model example of deriving a window objective from the task, not choosing one by habit. [§2.6.3, pp. 45–47]

Welch overlap is not free independent data: tapering the overlapping endpoints partly decorrelates segment estimates, which explains why the practical variance gain is real but not dramatic. [§2.7.2, p. 51]
Daniell’s warning punctures a common zero-padding illusion: averaging more densely sampled bins need not lower variance because those new bins become increasingly correlated. [§2.7.3, p. 53]

Apodization borrows its name from optics—removing the ‘feet’ of a diffraction pattern—and chooses between high-resolution and low-leakage windows at every frequency. In the two-tone example it inherits the best behavior of both. [§2.8.3, pp. 59–64, Figure 2.5]

A raw two-signal coherency estimate is always exactly one, no matter how unrelated the records are, because the unsmoothed outer-product matrix has rank one. This is an exceptionally sharp demonstration of why smoothing is essential. [§2.8.4, p. 64]
The book refuses to oversell the uncertainty principle: the 1/N resolution barrier belongs to nonparametric finite-window filtering, while correct parametric structure can surpass it. [§2.8.5, p. 68]

The shrinkage exercise halves the periodogram before doing anything sophisticated and thereby halves asymptotic MSE—a compact lesson that deliberate bias can beat an unbiased estimator. [Exercise 2.10, pp. 74–75]
Plotting in dB is statistically useful, not cosmetic: when variance scales with φ², log power gives an uncertainty band of constant width across frequency. [Exercise 2.12, p. 75]

The computer sequence moves from controlled two-tone experiments to 50-run Monte Carlo studies and finally to sunspot and Canadian lynx records, asking whether logarithmic detrending makes the lynx cycle more sinusoidal. [Exercises C2.19–C2.23, pp. 80–85]
